notes:
Here are my notes on Jeremiah 52, verse by verse. There are gaps you should know about first:

- **Sources I couldn't use.** I didn't get to netbible.org's notes, to any Catholic or Orthodox site (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), or to any Lutheran or Pentecostal-specific site. I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
- **No real Protestant split.** None of the pages I read showed the traditions disagreeing over any verse. The nearest thing is a difference over *how* God was involved in Zedekiah's sin (v. 3), shown below.
- **Enduring Word cut off.** The page stopped at v. 26. For vv. 27–34 I only have its summary.

**Introduction (whole chapter)**
- Several commentators think someone else wrote this chapter, perhaps Baruch. Clarke says the style isn't Jeremiah's: this writer spells the king "Jehoiachin," while Jeremiah always uses "Jeconiah" or "Coniah." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/
- Poole (Puritan) says it's generally held that Jeremiah didn't write it. He wouldn't have repeated chapter 39 at such length, and vv. 31–34 happened after his time. Some think it was added as a preface to Lamentations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/52.htm
- On the other side, Arend Remmers says the appendix was added under the Holy Spirit's guidance, "maybe even by the prophet Jeremiah himself." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/jeremiah.html
- Constable: events proved Jeremiah right and the false prophets wrong, so this closing chapter vindicates his ministry. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-52.html
- Following Keil, Coffman says this chapter and 2 Kings share a common source that described Judah's fall more fully. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-52.html
- Trapp (quoted by Guzik) notes that the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) adds a heading showing Jeremiah weeping over Jerusalem. This ties the chapter to Lamentations, and Jews are said to read them together on the 9th of Ab, the anniversary of the city's fall. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Nebuchadnezzar made young Zedekiah his puppet king and changed his name from Mattaniah (2 Kings 24:17). "Zedekiah" means "The Lord is Righteous," and God's righteous judgment was about to fall. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/
- Keil: vv. 1–3 match 2 Kings 24:18–20 word for word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik, citing Wiseman on 2 Chronicles 36: Zedekiah's evil was refusing God's word through Jeremiah, breaking an oath sworn in the Lord's name, and letting idolatry back into the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/

**v. 3** (how God was involved in Zedekiah's rebellion)
- Guzik: God's patience had run out, and He "allowed – even prompted" Babylon's conquest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/
- Poole goes further in the other direction. Zedekiah's sin is linked to God's wrath, but God did *not* put the wickedness in his heart; He let him fail. Poole adds that God often lets rulers fail because of their people's sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/52.htm
- An unnamed commentary on Bible Hub's v. 1 page says Zedekiah being "given over" was God's punishment for past sin, yet he stayed fully responsible for what he did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-1.htm
- Matthew Henry: no one is cast out of God's presence who hasn't first thrown himself out by sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-1.htm
- Utley (bible.org): "His presence" literally means "face to face." God wants to cast away our sins, not us. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-52
- Maclaren (quoted by Guzik) notes how calmly the event is told. God's wrath is named once as the cause, and the rest is plain fact. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/

**vv. 4–6**
- Guzik: a siege wall cut off trade so the city would starve into surrender. Feinberg notes the Old Testament tells this event four times. Maclaren says eighteen months of agony are packed into three verses. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/
- Bridgeway links the famine (v. 6) to people dying of hunger and disease, as Lamentations describes. https://studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/52-30.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says bread is God's gift, and here it is withheld as punishment for sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-52.html

**v. 7**
- Utley: the text doesn't say how the wall was breached, but it suggests siege machines (battering rams) broke a gate or section of wall. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-52
- Guzik describes the escape as a secret breakout using a decoy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/

**v. 8**
- Dilday (via Guzik): there is irony in the place. Israel's first victory in the land came at Jericho, and the last Davidic king was captured there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/

**v. 9**
- Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship): Riblah guarded a key international road. Nebuchadnezzar brought Zedekiah there. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/riblah/
- The Restoration Commentary suggests Nebuchadnezzar may have read out the curses Zedekiah swore on himself when he signed his loyalty treaty. If so, Zedekiah in effect sentenced himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-52.html
- Precept Austin: this was Nebuchadnezzar's formal sentence, but ultimately God's judgment carried out through Babylon. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary

**vv. 10–11**
- Keil: only Jeremiah 52 mentions the princes being executed at Riblah and Zedekiah being kept in prison until he died. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-1.htm
- Guzik: the blinding fulfilled Ezekiel 12:13, that he would go to Babylon but not see it. Knapp cites Josephus that Zedekiah was later buried magnificently, which fits Jeremiah 34:5. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/
- Precept Austin: "spiritual blindness led to literal blindness," and the two prophecies fit together perfectly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary

**v. 12**
- 2 Kings 25:8 says the "seventh" day; this verse says the "tenth." Commentators handle it differently:
  - Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Nebuzaradan left Riblah on the seventh and arrived on the tenth.
  - Geneva Study Bible: the fire began on the seventh and burned until the tenth.
  - Keil, Ellicott, the Cambridge Bible, and Blaney (quoted by Benson): a copyist's error, and we can't tell which day is right.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-12.htm
- Benson and Gill: this date is the origin of the fifth-month fast (Zechariah 7:3–5; 8:19). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-12.htm
- Cundall: the "19th year" here and the "18th year" in v. 29 differ because one count includes Nebuchadnezzar's accession year. Dilday says Nebuzaradan's title literally means "chief executioner." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Solomon's temple stayed in ruins until the returned exiles rebuilt it in Ezra's day. He also cites the Talmud's tradition that the Babylonians feasted in the temple before burning it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/
- Benson: Josephus says the temple had stood 470 years; Ussher counts 424. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-12.htm

**v. 14**
- Guzik: the walls stayed broken until Nehemiah rebuilt them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/

**vv. 15–16**
- Guzik: this was the third major wave of exile; only the poor were left. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/

**vv. 17–23**
- Coffman and Poole: the detailed list shows Jeremiah 27:16–22 (esp. v. 19) being fulfilled. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-52.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/52.htm
- Coffman on v. 20: there was too much bronze for any scale of the time to weigh. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-52.html
- Thompson (via Guzik): the list is a summary, not a technical record. It stresses how much bronze there was and how beautiful the pillars were, which made losing them more tragic. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/
- Bible Hub's study notes: the temple items were reminders of God's presence, so removing them signals His glory leaving (compare Ezekiel 10). https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/52.htm
- Matthew Henry: remembering their beauty shows all the more how evil sin is. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-12.htm
- Keil: the extra detail on the pillar decorations (v. 23) appears nowhere else in the Old Testament. Poole: v. 21 agrees with 1 Kings 7:15. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-12.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/52.htm

**v. 24**
- Poole: this Seraiah is the son of Azariah (1 Chronicles 6:14), not the Seraiah of 51:59. The "second priest" (Zephaniah) is the one in Jeremiah 21:1 and 29:25. The three doorkeepers were probably the most senior ones. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/52.htm

**v. 25**
- The Restoration Commentary thinks the sixty "people of the land" were conscripted soldiers executed as a warning. Coffman suggests they were wealthy aristocrats who backed the rebellion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-52.html ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-52.html

**vv. 26–27**
- The Restoration Commentary: Nebuzaradan picked those most responsible for the long resistance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-52.html
- Coffman reads "struck them down" as a beating before execution. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-52.html
- Bible Odyssey: many of Judah's leading officials were executed at Riblah. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/riblah/

**vv. 28–30**
- The text: Barnes and the Cambridge Bible say the Septuagint and 2 Kings lack these verses. Benson notes all other ancient versions and the Hebrew manuscripts include them, so they are genuine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-28.htm
- The "seventh year" (v. 28):
  - One view: this is Jehoiachin's exile of 597 BC, overlapping the "eighth year" of 2 Kings (Gill, Poole, Geneva, Constable).
  - Another view: "ten" dropped out of the text, so read "seventeenth," a deportation during the siege. This is held by Ellicott, Pulpit (following Ewald and Keil), the Cambridge Bible, and Barnes, who calls it "now generally received."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-28.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/52-28.html
- The low totals: Constable and Coffman suggest only adult men or heads of families were counted. Poole and Wesley (Methodist) compare the figure with the census in Numbers and infer how many were killed by sword, famine and disease. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/52-28.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/52.htm ; https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-jeremiah/
- Constable suggests the writer may have listed three deportations rather than four because three signified God's complete work. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-52.html
- Clarke dates the 23rd-year deportation to when Nebuchadnezzar was besieging Tyre. https://studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/52-28.html

**v. 31**
- The date: the "25th" here versus the "27th" in 2 Kings 25:27. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown suggests the decree was issued on the 25th and carried out on the 27th. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-31.htm
- Gill says the name "Evil" was a nickname meaning "foolish," and calls the reason for the release "not easy to say." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-31.htm
- Ellicott on 2 Kings: Jehoiachin was now 55. Pulpit thinks the release was probably part of a wider amnesty marking the new reign. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/25-27.htm
- The Pulpit homilies (Spanish version on StudyLight) suggest Daniel may have influenced the new king. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/52-15.html
- Pulpit: Ewald thought the exiles saw Jehoiachin as their rightful king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/52-31.htm

**vv. 32–34** (ending on hope)
- Ligonier (Reformed): this is not an incidental detail but a hopeful sign that David's throne was not forgotten. https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/davids-throne-endures
- Guzik's summary: a deliberate closing note that God hadn't abandoned His people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-52/
- Constable adds a caution. Jeremiah had said none of Jehoiachin's sons would rule (22:24–30), so carrying on David's line would need a supernatural act of God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-52.html
- Bible Hub sees God keeping the line alive despite that curse, with the hope finally fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 1:11–12). https://biblehub.com/q/Why_was_Jehoiachin_freed_in_Jeremiah_52_31.htm
- Pulpit's homilies note Jehoiachin was never given back his kingdom; at best he was an honoured subject of Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/52-15.html
- Poole: Jehoiachin died a captive but not a prisoner, unlike his father Jehoiakim and his uncle Zedekiah. He also draws a lesson in treating fallen people humanely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/52.htm
- The Restoration Commentary: conquered kings were seated in the Babylonian king's dining hall as a show of his power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-52.html
